name: Device Baseline
brief:
Not scored in the Cisco Networking Challenge, and worth knowing anyway. Every real device gets the same opening moves: a name, a secret, line passwords, a banner, and a save.

This is also the fastest way to learn what `copy running-config startup-config` is for, because the last task reloads the router.
watchFor: `enable secret` and `enable password` are not the same thing. The secret is hashed in the configuration file; the password is not, unless you turn on password encryption.

tasks.text: Set the privileged EXEC secret to class.
Set a console line password of cisco and require login on it.
Do the same for the vty lines 0 through 4.
Turn on password encryption so the plaintext line passwords stop appearing in the configuration.
tasks.hint: `service password-encryption`. Run show running-config before and after and compare.

tasks.text: Set a message-of-the-day banner containing the word Authorized.
tasks.hint: `banner motd #Authorized access only#` — the # is a delimiter, not part of the message.

tasks.text: Reload the router and confirm the hostname survived.
tasks.hint: If you skipped the save, everything you just did is gone. That is the lesson.

extension: Do the whole baseline again from a reset, timed, without looking at the hints. Aim for under three minutes.
debrief:
Running-config is what the device is doing. Startup-config is what it will do after a power cut. They are different files and nothing keeps them in sync for you.

In a competition, `copy running-config startup-config` after each device is a habit that costs five seconds and has saved entire rounds.
